claims.text: The initial alloy composition is Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
Under conventional cooling, the alloy forms several primary non-eutectic crystalline phases during solidification.
The alloy exhibits a complex, multistep crystallization sequence.
High-power ultrasonic vibration during melt-quenching will disrupt embryonic crystalline-cluster formation.
Disruption of embryonic crystalline clusters will suppress extensive primary crystallization.
Suppressing primary crystallization through ultrasound will enhance amorphous-phase retention and thermal stability.
The ultrasonic treatment should operate at 20–40 kHz.
Ultrasonic power sufficient to induce acoustic cavitation should be applied throughout cooling from above the liquidus to below the glass-transition temperature.
The intervention is intended to operate during rapid melt-spinning at cooling rates above 10^4 K/s.
The intervention is also intended for slower-cooling intervals and controlled reheating cycles.
Acoustic cavitation enhances melt stirring and disrupts early-stage crystalline clusters.
Increased undercooling and hindered homogeneous nucleation favor a metastable amorphous phase over primary crystallization.
Ultrasonic treatment will decrease the extent of primary non-eutectic crystallization.
Ultrasonic treatment will widen the processing window for glass formation.
Enhanced amorphous retention and thermal stability will be evidenced by reduced DSC crystallization exotherms on reheating.
Without ultrasound, the alloy forms multiple primary crystalline phases during both rapid and moderate cooling.
Nonuniform ultrasonic energy or energy below the cavitation threshold may eliminate the predicted benefit.

contradictions.description: The intervention is framed as melt-quenching and the mediator as stirring of a melt, yet cavitation is specified throughout the range down to below Tg and during reheating. Below Tg the material is outside the stated melt regime, and reheating is not itself melt-quenching, so the proposed temporal and physical scope is internally inconsistent.
